title: Scale and Significance
subtitle: Small causes are required by large effects

blocks.html: Astronomical scales are bewildering to human intuition. Billions of stars, billions of galaxies, and structure so large that distance and time blur together. The Milky Way is said to be on the order of 100,000 lightyears across. Outside the astronomy lab, it is difficult to give such quantities meaning.

One lightyear is often introduced as the distance a beam of light can cross in a year. To imagine that, we might think of light speed—in one second, circling the Earth seven times or reaching two-thirds of the way to the Moon—and then expand that second into a year. A strain for any human imagination.

But a lightyear is not a distance in the way we commonly understand that term—as a length of space between two points coexisting at the same time. Einstein broke open the secret in 1905 that all times and distances are relative—measurements are specific to a particular three-dimensional reference frame. Hermann Minkowski followed Einstein's rationale to the conclusion that intuitive (Euclidean) space has no primitive existence at all. A division of spacetime into space and time only arises relative to a unique timelike observer; two points separated in space never exist at the same time.

For life on Earth, different measurements of time and space usually correspond closely enough to be workable because, in the big picture, we are all very nearby to one another and we are all moving in almost the same direction at almost the same speed all the time.

But at large scales, the intuitive picture breaks down rather dramatically. A lightyear does not act like a distance, but rather like a latency: the minimum time elapsed at point A before any signal sent from point B can be received.

For example, the Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million lightyears away, so that our telescopes tonight will collect light that left Andromeda 2.5 million Earth years ago. If one day after that light got on the road, the Andromeda galaxy underwent a sudden acceleration and began to approach us at 70% of light speed, that would mean the galaxy has already traveled 1.75 million light years by tonight. Its present distance in our frame of reference would be only 750,000 lightyears. Yet Andromeda would appear unchanged tonight; we would not see any sign of its new trajectory.

With our Earth, once the center of the universe, relegated to an afterthought in its own Solar System (0.0003% by mass), and facing the reality that we cannot really see what is happening out there, it is easy to derive a sense of human smallness and insignificance.
I propose that this feeling is unjustified: it hides a logical error.

c380dc14-bd09-4b18-bc10-0a294140565f.alt: Center of our Milky Way Galaxy, located in the constellation of Sagittarius, a 2MASS (Two Micron All-Sky Survey) image. In visible light the lion's share of stars are hidden behind thick clouds of dust. This obscuring dust becomes increasingly transparent at infrared wavelengths. This 2MASS image, covering a field roughly 10 x 8 degrees (about the area of your fist held out at arm's length) reveals multitudes of otherwise hidden stars, penetrating all the way to the central star cluster of the Galaxy. This central core, seen in the upper left portion of the image, is about 25,000 light years away and is thought to harbor a supermassive black hole. The reddening of the stars here and along the Galactic Plane is due to scattering by the dust; it is the same process by which the sun appears to redden as it sets. The densest fields of dust still show up in this mosaic. Also evident are several nebulae to the lower right, including the Cat's Paw Nebula. The 2MASS analysis software has identified and measured the properties of almost 10 million stars in this spectacular field alone. Image credit: 2MASS / G. Kopan, R. Hurt
